text:
A fat priest sat on a soft bed beside the brazier in a matted room, Sidoine pressed to him kissing, tender, white, beautiful, adorned. Through a crack I saw them drink the best wine night and day, laugh, play, kiss, caress, both naked when they pleased, and learned that against bitterness no life is better than ease.

Had good Gontier and beloved Helen tried this life, they would not rub toast with garlic condemned by love. I value least their curds, stew, and creams. Sleep beneath a rosebush? I prefer a soft bed I can sink into. Is that not reason's choice? No life is better than ease.

They live on brown bread—madness!—and drink only water all year. I want none of the birds chirping in meadows at such a price, though they sing my favorite songs. Let Franc Gontier frolic with Helen beneath the insect-filled rosebush if they like that life. But I think: for happiness, no life is better than ease.

Prince, end this debate: I add that in my obscure childhood I heard a gaunt bard say, “No life is better than ease.”

translation.title: The Replies to Franc Gontier
